extracted.intended_audience: general readers of literary-philosophical essays; writers and thinkers interested in the relation of belief, reason, and mental health
extracted.subtask_description: An expository/argumentative essay that evaluates schools of thought (materialism, scepticism, pragmatism, will-worship, mysticism) by their psychological/ethical effects — i.e., whether they keep people 'sane' or lead to moral/mental morbidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-simple materialistic explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialism as an explanation of the world has 'a sort of insane simplicity' — it may 'cover everything' and yet 'leave everything out.' The materialist cosmos can be 'smaller than our world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: systems that explain all phenomena in mechanical terms and thereby ignore 'real things of the earth' (fighting peoples, first love, fear upon the sea). Examples: Mr. McCabe as an able sincere materialist whose scheme is unconscious of 'alien energies and the large indifference of the earth.' Scoring note: a robust explanatory framework should not reduce or omit the richness of lived human experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge creeds by their effect on health (psychological consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The present concern is not objective truth but the relation of beliefs/creeds to mental health: some complete explanations may be 'unhealthy' even if they 'explain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: When evaluating a belief-system, consider whether its completeness tends to destroy 'hope, courage, poetry, initiative' and other human qualities. Example contrast: the madman and the thoroughgoing materialist both have exhaustive explanations but share the same kind of 'incompleteness' in human terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow plurality and miscellany in your worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: A sane worldview 'admits that the universe is manifold and even miscellaneous,' recognizing that a sane person is complex (a touch of beast, devil, saint, citizen, madman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: systems that issue absolute vetoes (e.g., forbidding 'the slightest speck of spiritualism or miracle'). Good systems permit anomalies and tiny exceptions ('the tiniest imp... hiding in a pimpernel'). Practical test: does the system tolerate contradictions and human complexity?

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mystery and paradox — mysticism as psychological health
rubrics_metrics.description: Mysticism keeps men sane: 'As long as you have mystery you have health; when you destroy mystery you create morbidity.' The mystic 'allows one thing to be mysterious, and everything else becomes lucid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive pattern: allow a central, sacred mystery (a 'seed of dogma in a central darkness') which enables clear, humane action in daily life. Symbols: contrast circle (reason/madness) with cross (mystery/health) — the cross's paradoxical centre allows growth. Anti-pattern: excessive intellectual lucidity that eliminates mystery and thereby 'makes everything mysterious.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use reason 'without root' — ground thought in first principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief mark of insanity is 'reason used without root, reason in the void.' Thinking that begins 'at the wrong end' (without proper first principles) leads to madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: ensure that reasoning has foundational commitments or faiths that make thought possible; watch for abstracted logic that severs from human realities. Practical sign: when arguments, however logically consistent, result in lives that are 'manifest mistake[s]' they indicate rootless reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept genuine contradictions — cultivate 'stereoscopic' sight
rubrics_metrics.description: A sane spiritual sight is 'stereoscopic': 'If he saw two truths that seemed to contradict each other, he would take the two truths and the contradiction along with them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: value the capacity to hold simultaneous truths (e.g., fate and free will; children as kingdom of heaven yet obedient to earth). Anti-pattern: forcing artificial consistency by dropping truths to avoid paradox; scoring: higher health for frameworks that integrate contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve belief in free will and moral agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinism/fatalism tends to 'destroy humanity' by eliminating hope, courage, poetry, initiative, and the practical ability to praise, punish, or exhort — the determinist 'is not free to raise, to curse, to thank... or to say "thank you" for the mustard.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: a doctrine that denies moral agency undermines everyday moral practices (encouragement, exhortation, punishment aimed at reform). Anti-pattern: doctrines that reduce moral appeals to mere environmental manipulation ('he can put him in boiling oil; for boiling oil is an environment').

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that some authority (institutional/symbolic) defends reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious authority and institutional structures were historically 'organized for the difficult defence of reason' — not merely to suppress thought but to protect the human authority to think across generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: when evaluating calls to abolish or flatten authority, weigh the role authority plays in preserving the conditions for reason (education, transmission, and barriers against nihilistic scepticism). Anti-pattern: tearing down all authority without providing safeguards that sustain collective reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain stable categories/objects — thinking requires separable things
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremes that deny the existence of distinct things (radical flux or extreme uniqueness) attack thought itself: 'You cannot think if there are no things to think about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example critique: over-extreme interpretations of evolution or assertions like 'All chairs are quite different' (Mr. H.G. Wells) make classification and connecting of ideas impossible. Practical criterion: a usable worldview leaves enough identity/categories to allow generalization and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extreme pragmatism that denies objective truth
rubrics_metrics.description: While pragmatism can be useful 'as a preliminary guide to truth,' extreme pragmatism that tells a man to 'think what he must think and never mind the Absolute' is destructive because one necessary human need is belief in objective truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: pragmatist methods should include, not exclude, the conviction that some objective truths matter; anti-pattern: treating truth as wholly subordinate to mere utility or human need, thereby eliminating the 'Absolute' required for sustained reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place humility on ambition, not on conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Humility was meant to restrain appetite and ambition (making the world large by making oneself small). The modern misplacement of modesty 'upon the organ of conviction' makes people doubtful about aims and halts progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: distinguish healthy humility (doubt about one's efforts, spurring work) from poisonous humility (doubt about one's aims, causing stopping). Anti-pattern: intellectual modesty that undermines belief in truth or the possibility of learning from Nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject abstract worship of Will — will must be particular and measurable
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'worship of will' (praising will in general) is paradoxically 'the negation of will'; admiring will in general refuses concrete choice and standards and so paralyzes genuine volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: evaluate acts by particular standards (happiness, truth, law), not by amorphous appeals to 'will' as an end. Anti-patterns: doctrines that make 'choice' an abstract ideal ('will something' as though any will is equally valuable) and thus preclude moral comparison or praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance reason and mysticism for human flourishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Healthy thought requires a balance: reason without mysticism leads to sterile lucidity and madness; mysticism without reason is blind. The cross (paradox at centre) symbolizes a system that can grow without losing shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: adopt frameworks that combine grounded first principles (to root reason) with an allowance for mystery and paradox (to preserve humane qualities). Scoring: systems that enable growth, practical clarity, and preserve wonder score highest for 'health.'
